title: Every season of a Jewish life
hookLine: Jewish tradition marks every stage from birth to death
carry: each season of life is marked and blessed

cards: Pencil lines climb a kitchen doorframe. Each one has a name and a date beside it, scratched in on a birthday or the first day of school. Some families do this without being told to.
They want to mark the moments when a life moves up a notch, so they don't slip by unnoticed. Judaism has its own doorframe, and it runs from a life's first days to its last, and beyond.
Before stopping at any one mark, a look at the whole frame.

teach.b: First, the seasons. Ecclesiastes says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." And then: "A time to be born, and a time to die."

The tradition takes the seasons of a life seriously enough to give each one a ritual. Second, the marks. A new baby is welcomed with blessings and a name; for boys, with a covenant ceremony, the brit milah.
A young person comes of age as a bar or bat mitzvah, a son or daughter of the commandments.

teach.h: BIRTH, COMING OF AGE, CANOPY, MOURNING.
teach.b: Two people marry under a canopy, the chuppah. And at the end there are rituals for dying, for burial, and for the mourners who stay behind: days of sitting at home, called shiva, and the words of the kaddish.
Third, a map in the Mishnah.

In Ethics of the Fathers, Judah ben Tema lays out a life by ages: at five, scripture; at ten, Mishnah; at thirteen, the commandments; at eighteen, the wedding canopy; and on, through strength, understanding and counsel, to old age.
It isn't a schedule anyone must keep. It's a picture of a life with stages, each with its own work. Fourth, one blessing for many doorways.
Jewish tradition has a short blessing called shehecheyanu, said at new and joyful moments: a first fruit of the season, a holiday's first night, a new home, a new garment.
It thanks God for keeping us alive and bringing us to this time.
The rituals don't make the moments happen. They make sure a person stops, and notices, that they have.

how: Jewish life-cycle rituals are usually led by family and community together: a baby's naming in the synagogue or at home, a bar or bat mitzvah's first reading from the Torah, a wedding under the chuppah, and shiva, when mourners receive visitors at home.

games.q: what does “a life has rituals” mean?
o: a single ceremony held when a person turns forty

it marks birth, coming of age, marriage and mourning, with a blessing for new moments in between.
the Mishnah lays out a life by ages, from five to old age
Judah ben Tema, in Ethics of the Fathers: five for scripture, thirteen for the commandments, eighteen for the canopy.

it's said at new and joyful moments, like a holiday's first night or a new home.

games.q: Judah ben Tema's map of a life reaches age thirteen. what is that age for, in the Mishnah?
games.why: at thirteen, the commandments. it's the age behind bar mitzvah; the canopy comes at eighteen, and counsel later in the list.

practice: Start at the beginning of your own life, as far back as you know: a naming, a blessing, a party, a photo, then a birthday that mattered, a graduation, a first job, a move, a wedding, a funeral you stood at.
Let each mark come up like a pencil line on the doorframe, and notice which ones had a ritual and which passed with nothing to mark them. Notice, too, the next doorway ahead of you.

wordCard.voice: A life has rituals: birth, coming of age, marriage, mourning, each stage marked, and one blessing for the new moments in between. Today's word.
